# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

value.markup:
Remember when every phone had its own charger? A drawer full of cables, none of which fit the device in your hand. That's roughly where AI tooling was until recently: every assistant needed a custom integration for every system it wanted to talk to, and every integration was built, maintained and broken separately.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) fixes that the way USB did. It's an open standard that describes how an AI client discovers and calls tools exposed by a server. Write one MCP server for your system, and any MCP-capable assistant can use it, with no bespoke glue code per client.

Remember when every phone had its own charger? A drawer full of cables, none of which fit the device in your hand. That's roughly where AI tooling was until recently: every assistant needed a custom integration for every system it wanted to talk to, and every integration was built, maintained and broken separately.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) fixes that the way USB did. It's an open standard that describes how an AI client discovers and calls tools exposed by a server. Write one MCP server for your system, and any MCP-capable assistant can use it, with no bespoke glue code per client.

This very blog is a small proof of the idea. The document types, the block grid, the images in the media library and the pages themselves were all created by an AI assistant talking to Umbraco over MCP. Nobody clicked through the backoffice.

Two servers split the work along a line that makes sense to humans too: a developer-facing server for schema (data types, document types, templates, media and domains) and an editor-facing server for pages, blocks and publishing.

value.markup:
Tools that describe themselves

The clever part is discovery. An MCP server doesn't just expose endpoints; it publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a plain-language description and a JSON schema for its inputs. The assistant reads that list and works out for itself which tool fits the task, the same way a person skims a menu.

That means the knowledge of how to use a system lives with the system, written by the people who know it best, rather than being re-learned by every client that wants to talk to it.

value.markup:
Guardrails come with the territory

Because every action goes through a named tool with a typed input, MCP keeps an assistant on the rails. It can't wander off and poke the database directly; it can only do what the server offers, and the server can ask a human to confirm anything destructive before it happens.

The tools also teach. When a call fails, a good server explains why in a sentence, and the assistant fixes its input and tries again. Building this site involved exactly that loop, and it's a far nicer way to work than reading a stack trace.

The result is a CMS that people and assistants can share: editors keep the backoffice they know, and the repetitive setup work can be handed to an assistant that speaks the same protocol as everything else.

content.text:
The blog is built and running. The front page and both posts each return 200, every block renders, and none of them contain "Could not render component". Umbraco is still running in the background so you can look at it.

**How to view it**
- Front page: https://localhost:44317/
- Post 1: https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome/
- Post 2: https://localhost:44317/building-a-website-by-conversation/
- Backoffice: https://localhost:44317/umbraco (admin@example.com / 1234567890)

**Schema (umbraco server)**
- **Blocks** (in the Blocks folder):
  - `richTextBlock`: text.
  - `imageBlock`: image and caption.
  - `quoteBlock`: quote and attribution.
- **Block grid**: a data type called "Blog Body Block Grid" that allows those three blocks.
- **Page types** (in the Pages folder), each with its own template:
  - `blogFrontPage`: title, intro and a block-grid body.
  - `blogPost`: title, publish date, excerpt, listing image and a block-grid body.
- **Allowed children**: Site Root → Blog Front Page → Blog Post. I read each type back to confirm it saved.
- **Media**: a "Blog" folder with 4 photos from `unsplash/`. The image captions credit the photographers.
- **Domain**: `/` on the front page (not WWW). I read it back to confirm.

**Content (umbraco-editor server)**
- **Front page**: a "Blog" page under WWW with one rich text block. It lists the posts newest first, each with its image, date, title and excerpt.
- **"Why MCP Is Awesome"**: 5 blocks (rich text, image, rich text, quote, rich text).
- **"Building a Website by Conversation"**: 4 blocks (rich text, image, quote, rich text).
- All three pages are published, and `get-page` shows their values. uSync exported the new types, templates and content.

**Code**
- Two page templates that render the body with `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`.
- One file per block in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/`, each starting with `@inherits UmbracoViewPage<BlockGridItem<TheBlock>>` and only passing data to its component.
- One ViewComponent per block in `ViewComponents/`, with its view in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
- Plain view models in `Models/Blocks/`.
- `dotnet build` passes with 0 warnings and 0 errors. `npm run build` produced `site.css`, and I checked that it contains the classes used in the views.
- All image URLs are built with `GetCropUrl()`. Each image URL and `site.css` returned 200 with the correct content type.

**Problems**
- The first publish, which tried to publish the front page and its child posts together, came back "Publish cancelled" from the confirmation step. Publishing each page separately worked.
- I only checked the pages with curl; I didn't look at the styling in a browser.
- The two templates are standalone HTML pages with no shared layout, so the header markup is repeated in both.
- Umbraco's output goes to `.umbraco-run.log` in the solution folder. Stop the background `dotnet run` when you're done.
